title: Conformal Mapping, Branches, and the Schwarz Lemma

items.title: Dictionary for holomorphic logarithm branches, the principal logarithm, and principal powers
Complex powers defined from a holomorphic logarithm branch
Branch-defined complex powers agree with integer powers
items.strategy: Use the defining identity $\exp(L(z)) = z$ together with the complex exponential addition formula to collapse repeated branch powers to the already-published integer powers.

items.title: On positive reals, the principal branch power agrees with the published real power
items.strategy: For $x > 0$, the principal logarithm equals the real logarithm. Substituting that identity into the branch-power definition recovers the published real-power definition word for word.

items.title: Different branches shift logarithms by $2\pi i k$ and complex powers by roots of unity
items.strategy: Subtract two logarithm branches, exponentiate the difference, and use the kernel description of the exponential map. The power discrepancy then follows by applying the exponential addition formula to $\alpha(L_1-L_2)$.

items.title: Conformal equivalence and the automorphism group of a domain
The unit disc, the upper half-plane, and Blaschke factors
Blaschke factors are automorphisms of the disc
items.strategy: Check the boundary-modulus identity for $\varphi_a(z) = (a-z)/(1-\overline{a}z)$ on $|z|=1$, use the maximum principle to keep the image inside the disc, and compute the inverse directly.

items.title: Schwarz lemma with the equality cases
items.strategy: Apply the maximum principle to $f(z)/z$ after removing the removable singularity at the origin. The equality cases are exactly the interior-maximizer cases for the maximum principle.

items.title: Schwarz-Pick lemma on the unit disc
items.strategy: Conjugate an arbitrary disc self-map by the Blaschke automorphisms that move one chosen point and its image to the origin, apply Schwarz's lemma there, and rewrite the conclusion in pseudohyperbolic and derivative form.

items.title: Every automorphism of the disc is a rotated Blaschke factor
items.strategy: Move the zero of the automorphism to the origin with a Blaschke factor, apply the rigid equality case in the Schwarz lemma, and move back.

items.title: Automorphisms of the upper half-plane are real Mobius maps
items.strategy: Conjugate by the Cayley transform to transfer the disc-automorphism classification to the upper half-plane, then simplify the resulting formula to the $PSL_2(\mathbb R)$ form and verify the converse directly from the imaginary-part formula.

items.title: The Poincare metric and distance on the unit disc
The Poincare distance has the formula $2\operatorname{artanh}|\varphi_z(w)|$ and is disc-automorphism invariant
items.strategy: Move one point to the origin with a Blaschke factor, integrate the metric along radial segments to identify the distance there, and then use the disc-automorphism classification to transport the formula to all pairs of points.

items.title: Biholomorphisms are conformal and have holomorphic inverse
Conformal equivalence is an equivalence relation
items.strategy: Identity maps, inverse maps, and compositions of biholomorphisms give the three clauses directly from the definition.

items.title: Power maps are biholomorphisms on sectors of width less than $2\pi/n$
items.strategy: Choose a logarithm branch on the sector, write $z^n$ as $\exp(nL(z))$, and use the branch width to show injectivity and to identify the inverse sector by division of the argument interval.

items.title: A slit-plane root branch biholomorphically parametrizes a sector
items.strategy: Write the root branch as $\exp(\operatorname{Log}(z)/n)$ on the slit plane and read its image from the principal-argument interval. The inverse is the appropriate power map on the target sector.

items.title: The principal logarithm is a biholomorphism from the slit plane to the principal strip
items.strategy: Use the published holomorphy of the principal logarithm on the slit plane, identify its image from the principal-argument normalization, and check injectivity by the classification of complex logarithms.

items.title: The exponential is the inverse biholomorphism from the principal strip to the slit plane
items.strategy: Compose the principal logarithm with the exponential in both orders, using the strip bound on the imaginary part to force the principal branch and recover exact inversion.

items.title: The Joukowski map is a biholomorphism from the exterior disc onto $\mathbb{C}\setminus[-1,1]$
items.strategy: Differentiate $J(z) = (z + z^{-1})/2$ to locate the critical points, check that they stay off the exterior domain, and build the inverse from the holomorphic square root branch of $w^2-1$ on the complement of the segment.

items.title: The sine map biholomorphically sends an upper half-strip onto the upper half-plane
items.strategy: Rewrite sine as a Mobius transform of $e^{2iz}$, identify the exponential image of the half-strip, and compute the final Mobius image explicitly.

items.title: The sphere, the plane, and the disc are pairwise non-biholomorphic
items.strategy: Use compactness and open mapping to separate the sphere from the noncompact models, and use Liouville's theorem to rule out a biholomorphism between the plane and the bounded disc.

title: Conformal Mapping, Branches, and the Schwarz Lemma — Examples

items.title: The principal logarithm fails to turn multiplication into addition at $(-1,-1)$
items.strategy: Compute the two principal logarithms and compare $\operatorname{Log}((-1)(-1))$ with $\operatorname{Log}(-1) + \operatorname{Log}(-1)$ directly.

items.title: The principal square root fails to respect products at $(-1,-1)$
items.strategy: Evaluate the principal square roots of $-1$, of $(-1)(-1)$, and compare the two sides explicitly on the declared principal branch.

items.title: A horizontal strip is mapped biholomorphically to the disc by an exponential and a Cayley transform
items.strategy: Map the strip to the upper half-plane by the exponential and then to the disc by the Cayley transform, checking the boundary correspondence on both steps.

items.title: A disc automorphism carrying one prescribed point to another
items.strategy: Compose the two Blaschke factors that move the source point to the origin and the origin to the target point, and simplify the resulting formula.

items.title: A power map sends a sector to a half-plane
items.strategy: Choose a sector whose doubled angle interval is exactly $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ and apply the sector-power theorem with that normalization.

items.title: The Joukowski map sends circles centered at the origin to ellipses
items.strategy: Parameterize the source circle, apply the Joukowski formula, and isolate the resulting real and imaginary parts to read off the ellipse equation.

items.title: Boundary tracking for the sine biholomorphism of the upper half-strip
items.strategy: Follow the vertical sides and the real boundary of the half-strip under the sine map and compare them with the real-axis boundary of the upper half-plane.

items.title: Complex conjugation preserves angle magnitudes but is not conformal
items.strategy: Compare the action of $z \mapsto \overline{z}$ on tangent directions. The map preserves the absolute angle but reverses orientation, so it fails the page's conformal convention.

items.title: FALSE: conformal maps preserve Euclidean lengths
items.strategy: Use a nontrivial rotation-scaled linear map or a simple disc automorphism to preserve angles while changing the length of a tangent vector.

items.title: FALSE: Schwarz's lemma remains true without the hypothesis $f(0)=0$
items.strategy: Use a disc automorphism that moves the origin. It is still a holomorphic self-map of the disc, but it violates the modulus and derivative conclusions centered at zero.

title: Infinite Products and the Weierstrass Factorisation Theorem

items.title: Dictionary for using the published infinite-product definition over $\mathbb{C}$
Absolute convergence criterion for complex infinite products
items.strategy: Translate the product to the deviations from $1$, compare the convergence problem with the published real criterion for $\prod (1 + |a_n|)$, and use the same tail estimates pointwise in $\mathbb{C}$.

items.title: Normal convergence of holomorphic products
Normally convergent products define holomorphic functions with the expected zeros
items.strategy: Take logarithmic deviations from $1$, use the compact-uniform absolute control to apply the Weierstrass convergence theorem to the partial products, and then isolate the finite set of factors that can vanish on a given compact set.

items.title: The logarithmic derivative of a normally convergent product
items.strategy: Differentiate the partial products, divide by the nonvanishing limit away from the zero set, and pass to the locally uniform limit on compacta disjoint from the zeros.

items.title: Weierstrass elementary factors
The unit-disc estimate for Weierstrass elementary factors
items.strategy: Differentiate $1 - E_p(w)$ explicitly, identify its zero of order $p+1$ at the origin, and bound the normalized quotient on the closed unit disc.

items.title: Weierstrass products, canonical products, and genus
The exponent of convergence of a zero sequence
A canonical product converges when the $(p+1)$-power reciprocal sum converges
items.strategy: Apply the elementary-factor estimate to each compact set and compare the resulting majorant with the convergent reciprocal power series that defines the genus threshold.

items.title: Weierstrass product theorem on the complex plane
items.strategy: Choose the elementary-factor orders so that the reciprocal-power convergence criterion applies to the repeated nonzero zero-sequence, and multiply by the correct power of $z$ for the zero at the origin.

items.title: Weierstrass factorization for entire functions
items.strategy: Build an entire product with exactly the zeros of $f$, divide $f$ by it, and use the zero-free quotient to define the residual entire exponential factor.

items.title: Every meromorphic function on $\mathbb{C}$ is a quotient of entire functions
items.strategy: Cancel the pole divisor of the meromorphic function with an entire denominator provided by the Weierstrass product theorem, leaving an entire numerator.

items.title: The Weierstrass product for sine
items.strategy: Apply the factorization theorem to $\sin(\pi z)$, use its zero set and multiplicities, and determine the zero-free factor by comparing growth and the derivative at the origin.

items.title: Jensen's formula on a disc
items.strategy: Factor the zeros inside the disc, apply the harmonic mean-value relation to the zero-free quotient, and then remove the generic-radius restriction by a radial limiting argument.

items.title: Jensen's formula bounds the number of zeros in a smaller disc
items.strategy: Estimate each logarithmic zero term in Jensen's formula from below by the common smaller-radius contribution and solve for the zero count.

items.title: The order of an entire function
The zero-sequence exponent is at most the entire order
items.strategy: Insert the finite-order growth bound into Jensen's formula, derive a zero-count estimate, and convert that bound into convergence of reciprocal powers above the order.

items.title: Hadamard factorization for finite-order entire functions
items.strategy: Choose the canonical genus allowed by the zero-exponent bound, divide the entire function by the resulting canonical product, and prove the remaining entire logarithm has vanishing derivative above degree $\lfloor \rho \rfloor$.

items.title: A nonintegral order bounds the canonical genus by its floor
items.strategy: Read the polynomial degree and canonical genus bound off Hadamard's factorization and simplify when the order is not an integer.

title: Infinite Products and the Weierstrass Factorisation Theorem — Examples

items.title: The product $\prod_{n \ge 1}(1 + z/2^n)$ defines an entire zero-free function
items.strategy: Use the geometric-series bound on compacta to verify normal convergence of the deviations from $1$, and track the zero set factor by factor.

items.title: The sine product recovers the Basel sum
items.strategy: Compare the quadratic term in the Taylor expansion of $\sin(\pi z)/(\pi z)$ with the quadratic term in its Weierstrass product expansion.

items.title: Jensen's formula for a polynomial
items.strategy: Factor the polynomial into linear terms and substitute the factorization directly into Jensen's formula to read off the finite zero sum.

items.title: A genus-zero canonical product for zeros at the squares
items.strategy: Check the convergence of $\sum 1/n^2$ for the reciprocal-square zero sequence and apply the canonical-product convergence theorem with genus $0$.

items.title: A conditionally convergent linear term does not force a nonzero product limit
items.strategy: Apply the published signed infinite-product criterion to $a_n = (-1)^n/\sqrt{n+2}$, using the conditional convergence of the linear series and the divergence of the square series.

items.title: FALSE: Weierstrass factorization is unique
items.strategy: Multiply any valid factorization by $e^{g(z)}$ for a nonconstant entire function $g$ and compare the zero divisor with the unchanged function after adjusting the nonzero factor.

items.title: FALSE: every discrete zero sequence admits a genus-zero canonical product
items.strategy: Use the zero sequence at the positive integers, whose reciprocal first powers diverge, so the genus-zero product fails while the genus-one sine product succeeds.

items.title: FALSE: the order of an entire function always equals the canonical genus in its factorization
items.strategy: Compare a finite-order entire function such as $e^z$ or a polynomial with its trivial zero divisor: the function has positive or zero order while the canonical product has genus $0$.
